---
title: Ulrich Enterprises
output: pdf_document
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
library(scales)
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(101)
show_dist <- function(df, value_label, caption) {
    out <- rbind(Value       = value_label(df$value),
                 Probability = label_percent()(df$probability))
    knitr::kable(out, caption = caption, col.names = NULL, align = "r")
}
```

Dahlia Simmons, CFO of Ulrich Enterprises, is analyzing a new project to sell
solar powered batteries for cell phones. Dahlia has estimated the following
probability distribution for the variables in the project.

```{r project_description, echo = FALSE}
prob_industry_demand <- data.frame(
    probability = c(.1, .3, .4, .2),
    value       = c(80e6, 95e6, 108e6, 124e6)
)
show_dist(prob_industry_demand,
          label_number(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M"),
          caption = "Industry Demand")

prob_ulrich_market <- data.frame(
    probability = c(.05, .2, .2, .25, .2, .1),
    value       = c(.01, .02, .03, .04, .05, .06)
)
show_dist(prob_ulrich_market,
          label_number(scale = 100, suffix = "%"),
          caption = "Ulrich Market Share")

prob_initial_cost <- data.frame(
    probability = c(.2, .7, .1),
    value       = c(60e6, 65e6, 72e6)
)
show_dist(prob_initial_cost,
          label_number(scale = 1e-6, prefix = "$", suffix = "M"),
          caption = "Initial Cost")

prob_variable_cost_unit <- data.frame(
    probability = c(.2, .65, .15),
    value       = c(24, 26, 29)
)
show_dist(prob_variable_cost_unit,
          label_number(scale = 1, prefix = "$"),
          caption = "Variable Cost per unit")

prob_fixed_costs <- data.frame(
    probability = c(.15, .25, .4, .2),
    value       = c(20e6, 24e6, 27e6, 31e6)
)
show_dist(prob_fixed_costs,
          label_number(scale = 1e-6, prefix = "$", suffix = "M"),
          caption = "Fixed Costs")
```

The unit price depends on the industry demand since a greater demand will result in a higher price. Dahlia determines that the price per unit will be given by the equation:

$$
\text{Price} = \text{Industry demand}\ \ / \ \ 2{,}000{,}000\ \ +/- \$2
$$

The random "$+/- \$2$" term represents an increase or decrease in price
according to the following distribution:

```{r price_randomness, echo = FALSE}
price_randomness <- data.frame(
    probability = c(.45, .55),
    value       = c(-2, 2)
)
show_dist(price_randomness,
          label_number(scale = 1, prefix = "$"),
          caption = "Price Randomness")
```

The length of the project, tax rate, and required return are:

```{r project_variables, echo = FALSE}
time_span <- 6
tax_rate <- .34
required_return <- .14
view_project_variables <- data.frame(
    `Project Length (years)` = time_span,
    `Tax Rate`               = label_percent()(tax_rate),
    `Required Return`        = label_percent()(required_return),
    check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(t(view_project_variables))
```

a. Create a Monte Carlo simulation for the project with at least 500 runs.
   Calculate the IRR for each run.
b. Create a graph of the distribution of the IRRs from the Monte Carlo
   simulation for different ranges of IRR.
c. Create a graph for the cumulative probability function for the IRR distribution.

---

Below are each of the functions we will be using.

The first function is the present value interest factor for annuities. This is
used to compute the present value of a stream of the same payments. Just
multiply this factor by the cash flow.

```{r pvia}
pvia <- function(r, t) sum((1 + r)^(-(1:t)))
```

This function is used to calculate the price. Price is dependent on the
industry demand and the `price_randomness` factor.

```{r calculate_price}
calc_price <- function(industry_demand) {
    pr <- price_randomness
    randomness <- sample(pr$value, size = 1, prob = pr$probability)
    industry_demand / 2e6 + randomness
}
```

This function calculates the cash flow.

```{r calculate_cash_flow}
calc_cash_flow <- function(industry_demand, market_share, var_unit_cost,
                           fixed_costs, initial_costs, time_span, tax_rate) {
    units          <- market_share * industry_demand
    price          <- calc_price(industry_demand)
    revenues       <- price * units
    variable_costs <- units * var_unit_cost
    total_cost     <- variable_costs + fixed_costs
    depreciation   <- initial_costs / time_span
    pretax         <- revenues - total_cost - depreciation
    tax            <- pretax * tax_rate
    net_profit     <- pretax - tax
    cash_flow      <- net_profit + depreciation
    cash_flow
}
```

Finally we calculate the internal rate of return. We need to ensure that the
cash flows are positive, otherwise `uniroot` will fail because there is no sign
change and therefore there is no IRR. If cash flows are zero or negative we
return `NA`. We use an interval equivalent to -100\% to 1,000\% to ensure our
calculation is within range. `NA` runs count as failing the comparison with the
required rate of return.

```{r calculate_irr}
calc_irr <- function(initial_investment, cash_flow, time_span) {
    f <- function(r) -initial_investment + cash_flow * pvia(r, time_span)
    if (cash_flow <= 0) return(NA)
    uniroot(f, interval = c(-1, 10), tol = 1e-9)$root
}
```

This function runs the Monte Carlo simulations. Just specify the number of
iterations to run. The function first samples each of the variables:
`industry_demand`, `ulrich_market`, `initial_cost`, `variable_cost_unit`,
`fixed_costs`, and then calculates the `cash_flow` and then finally the `irr`.
Each irr outcome is collected in a vector and the vector of irr outcomes is
return. Each run of run_simulation draws once and applies the same cash flow
for each of the six years.

```{r run_simulation}
run_simulation <- function(iterations) {
    outcomes <- c()
    for(i in 1:iterations) {
        industry_demand <- sample(prob_industry_demand$value, size = 1,
                                  prob = prob_industry_demand$probability)
        ulrich_market <- sample(prob_ulrich_market$value, size = 1,
                                  prob = prob_ulrich_market$probability)
        initial_cost <- sample(prob_initial_cost$value, size = 1,
                                  prob = prob_initial_cost$probability)
        variable_cost_unit <- sample(prob_variable_cost_unit$value, size = 1,
                                  prob = prob_variable_cost_unit$probability)
        fixed_costs <- sample(prob_fixed_costs$value, size = 1,
                                  prob = prob_fixed_costs$probability)
        cash_flow <- calc_cash_flow(industry_demand, ulrich_market, variable_cost_unit,
                                    fixed_costs, initial_cost, time_span, tax_rate)
        irr <- calc_irr(initial_cost, cash_flow, time_span)
        outcomes <- c(outcomes, irr)
    }
    outcomes
}
irr_outcomes <- run_simulation(500)
mean_irr_positive_cf <- mean(irr_outcomes, na.rm = TRUE)
median_irr_positive_cf <- median(irr_outcomes, na.rm = TRUE)
prob_beats_required <- mean(irr_outcomes > required_return & !is.na(irr_outcomes))
neg_zero_run_rate <- mean(is.na(irr_outcomes))
```

Among runs with positive cash flow, the mean IRR is 
`r label_percent()(mean_irr_positive_cf)`. The median IRR is
`r label_percent()(median_irr_positive_cf)` for the same runs.
`r label_percent()(neg_zero_run_rate)` of the runs had zero or negative cash
flow every year and have no IRR. The probability that the project beats the
required rate of return of `r label_percent()(required_return)` is
`r label_percent()(prob_beats_required)`.

The distribution graph of the `irr_outcomes` is a simple histogram graph. We use
`geom_histogram` from `ggplot2` to render the distribution.

```{r histogram}
irr_df <- data.frame(irr = irr_outcomes[!is.na(irr_outcomes)])
ggplot(irr_df, aes(x = irr)) +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, boundary = 0, color = "white") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = required_return, linetype = "dashed") +
    annotate("text", x = required_return, y = Inf, vjust = 1.5, hjust = -0.1,
             label = paste0("required return (", label_percent()(required_return), ")"),
             size = 3) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = label_percent(),
                       breaks = seq(-0.75, 3, by = 0.25)) +
    labs(title = "Distribution of IRR",
         x = "IRR", y = "Number of runs",
         caption = paste0("Excludes ", label_percent()(neg_zero_run_rate),
                          " of runs with no IRR (zero or negative cash flow)."))
```

We can use `ggplot2::stat_ecdf` function to graph the cumulative distribution
function. The ECDF only includes runs that have an IRR, so its probabilities
are conditional on the cash flow being positive. At the
`r label_percent()(required_return)` required return, the curve's height is
`r label_percent(0.1)(mean(irr_df$irr <= required_return))`: the share of runs
_with an IRR_ that fall at or below the hurdle. The overall failure rate also
includes the `r label_percent()(neg_zero_run_rate)` of runs with no IRR which
also fail:

`r label_percent()(neg_zero_run_rate)` +
`r label_percent()(mean(!is.na(irr_outcomes)))` $\times$
`r label_percent(0.1)(mean(irr_df$irr <= required_return))` =
`r label_percent(0.1)(1 - prob_beats_required)`,

which matches the `r label_percent()(prob_beats_required)` probability of
beating the required return.

```{r cumulative_graph}
ggplot(irr_df, aes(x = irr)) +
    stat_ecdf(geom = "step") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = required_return, linetype = "dashed") +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = label_percent(),
                       breaks = seq(-0.75, 3, by = 0.25)) +
    labs(title = "Cumulative Distribution Function of IRR",
         x = "IRR",
         y = "P(IRR <= x)",
         caption = paste0("Excludes ", label_percent()(neg_zero_run_rate),
                          " of runs with no IRR (zero or negative cash flow)."))
```
